        "statement": "Let $n\\ge1$, let $U\\subseteq\\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\\theta_0\\in U$, and let $u\\in\\mathbb R^n$ satisfy $\\lVert u\\rVert_2=1$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be an open interval with $0\\in I$ and such that $\\gamma(\\theta):=\\theta_0+\\theta u\\in U$ for every $\\theta\\in I$. Let $F:U\\to\\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $F(\\theta_0)=0$, and suppose that for every $\\theta\\in I$ the directional derivative of $F$ along $u$ satisfies\n$$D_uF(\\theta_0+\\theta u)=\\langle\\nabla F(\\theta_0+\\theta u),u\\rangle\\ge m>0$$\n([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). Let a recorded scalar $\\hat y\\in\\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\\hat y|\\le s$ with $s\\ge0$, and let a calibration-error bound $|y-\\hat y|\\le\\delta$ with $\\delta\\ge0$ hold for $y:=F(\\theta_0+\\theta u)$ at a candidate $\\theta\\in I$. Then\n$$|\\theta|\\le\\frac{s+\\delta}{m},$$\nand the corresponding configuration displacement $\\gamma(\\theta)-\\theta_0=\\theta u$ has Euclidean length $\\lVert\\theta u\\rVert_2=|\\theta|$. The conclusion is a deterministic conditional statement about the stated bounds; it is not a sampling law, a statistical inference, or a claim about any historical report, and the parameters $s,\\delta,m$ are supplied by the user of the statement rather than estimated from data here.",
        "strategy": "Set $\\gamma(\\theta):=\\theta_0+\\theta u$ and $g:=F\\circ\\gamma:I\\to\\mathbb R$, and verify the hypotheses of the bounded-error model-comparison lemma for $g$ on $I$ before reading off its conclusion. (i) Each component $\\theta\\mapsto(\\theta_0)_j+\\theta u_j$ of $\\gamma$ is a sum of a constant and a scalar multiple of the identity $\\theta\\mapsto\\theta^1$, hence differentiable with derivative $u_j$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). These partial derivatives are the constant functions $u_j$, so they exist on the open interval $I$ and are continuous there; [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]] therefore makes $\\gamma$ totally differentiable at every $\\theta\\in I$ with $D\\gamma(\\theta)$ the linear map whose matrix is $J\\gamma(\\theta)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), that is, $D\\gamma(\\theta)(h)=hu$ for $h\\in\\mathbb R$. (ii) Both $F$ (on the open set $U$) and $\\gamma$ (on the open interval $I$) are covered by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]), so $g$ is totally differentiable at every $\\theta\\in I$ with $Dg(\\theta)=DF(\\gamma(\\theta))\\circ D\\gamma(\\theta)$. For a real-valued function on an open subset of $\\mathbb R$ the ordinary derivative is the total derivative applied to $1$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), so $g'(\\theta)=DF(\\gamma(\\theta))(u)=D_uF(\\gamma(\\theta))=\\langle\\nabla F(\\gamma(\\theta)),u\\rangle\\ge m$ by the hypothesis ([[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). (iii) The derivative $g'=\\sum_j(\\partial_jF\\circ\\gamma)\\,u_j$ is continuous on $I$: the partial derivatives $\\partial_jF$ are continuous on $U$ because $F$ is $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); $\\gamma$ is continuous because $d_2(\\gamma(\\theta),\\gamma(\\theta'))=\\lVert(\\theta-\\theta')u\\rVert_2=|\\theta-\\theta'|$ by the homogeneity of the Euclidean norm and $\\lVert u\\rVert_2=1$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[def-metric-continuity]]); each composite $\\partial_jF\\circ\\gamma$ is then continuous because for open $V\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ its preimage is $\\gamma^{-1}[\\partial_jF^{-1}[V]]$, the preimage under $\\gamma$ of an open set ([[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]]); and $g'$ is a finite sum of scalar multiples of these composite functions, hence continuous as a real function on $I$ ([[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]). Thus $g$ is $C^1$ on $I$ in the lemma's sense, and $g(0)=F(\\theta_0)=0$. (iv) Apply the bounded-error model-comparison lemma ([[lem-em-bounded-error-model-comparison]]) to $g$ on $I$ with lower bound $m>0$ and centre $0$: every candidate $\\theta\\in I$ whose model value $y=g(\\theta)=F(\\theta_0+\\theta u)$ satisfies $|\\hat y|\\le s$ and $|y-\\hat y|\\le\\delta$ obeys $|\\theta-0|\\le(s+\\delta)/m$. Finally $\\lVert\\theta u\\rVert_2=|\\theta|\\,\\lVert u\\rVert_2=|\\theta|$ by homogeneity of the Euclidean norm and $\\lVert u\\rVert_2=1$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). No probability model, sampling law or statistical inference is used at any step.",

        "statement": "(i) Specialise [[thm-em-uncertainty-analysis]] to $n=1$, $U=\\mathbb R$, $\\theta_0=0$, $u=1$, $I=\\mathbb R$ and $F(\\theta)=m\\theta$ with $m>0$. Then $F$ is $C^1$, $F(0)=0$, $\\nabla F(\\theta)=m$ and $\\langle\\nabla F(\\theta),1\\rangle=m\\ge m$, so the theorem's hypothesis holds with equality. Fix the recorded value $\\hat y=0$ (so $s=0$) and any $\\delta\\ge0$. A candidate $\\theta\\in\\mathbb R$ is compatible with the calibration bound exactly when $|F(\\theta)-\\hat y|=|m\\theta|\\le\\delta$, that is, exactly when $|\\theta|\\le\\delta/m$; this is precisely the theorem's bound $(s+\\delta)/m=\\delta/m$, and the bound is attained (equality) at $\\theta=\\pm\\delta/m$. Hence the constant $(s+\\delta)/m$ cannot be improved for this instance, and the special case $\\delta=0$ leaves $\\theta=0$ as the only compatible candidate. (ii) The positive lower bound on the response is not removable. If it is dropped, take $m=0$ and $F\\equiv0$ on $\\mathbb R$: the hypothesis $\\langle\\nabla F(\\theta),u\\rangle\\ge m>0$ fails, and with the same data $\\hat y=0$, $s=0$, $\\delta\\ge0$ every $\\theta\\in\\mathbb R$ is compatible, because $y=0$ and $|y-\\hat y|=0\\le\\delta$; no finite parameter bound then follows from the indicator and the two bounds alone. (iii) These are mathematical observations about a hypothetical bounded-error model: no experimental data, sampling law or statistical inference is used or asserted, and the displayed numbers are stipulated parameters, not measurements.",

Multiplying the inequality $|\\theta|\\le\\delta/m$ by $m>0$ gives $|m\\theta|\\le\\delta$ and conversely, using $|m\\theta|=m|\\theta|$ and the defining clauses of the absolute value ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]]); at $\\theta=\\pm\\delta/m$ one has $|m\\theta|=\\delta$, so equality holds in the bound while the candidate remains compatible; and for $\\delta=0$ the inequality $|m\\theta|\\le0$ forces $m\\theta=0$, hence $\\theta=0$.         "inventory_expansion_required": false,
        "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$), the convention of the Lebesgue interface used below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\\ge3$, let $\\Phi$ be the fundamental solution of $-\\Delta$ on $\\mathbb R^n$ normalised by $-\\Delta T_\\Phi=\\delta_0$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]), so that for $z\\ne0$\n$$\\Phi(z)=\\frac{|z|^{2-n}}{(n-2)\\omega_{n-1}},\\qquad \\nabla\\Phi(z)=-\\frac{z}{\\omega_{n-1}|z|^n},\\qquad |\\nabla\\Phi(z)|=\\frac{1}{\\omega_{n-1}|z|^{n-1}},$$\nlet $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R^n)$ be real, measurable and zero $\\lambda_n$-almost everywhere outside a closed ball $\\overline B_R(0)=\\{x:|x|\\le R\\}$ of finite radius $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let\n$$Nf(x)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\Phi(x-y)f(y)\\,d\\lambda_n(y)$$\nbe the Newtonian potential ([[def-newtonian-potential]]). Then:\n(a) [Representation and differentiability off the far field] for every $x\\in\\mathbb R^n$ with $|x|>2R$ the integral $\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\nabla\\Phi(x-y)f(y)\\,d\\lambda_n(y)$ is absolutely convergent, the function $Nf$ is differentiable at $x$ with\n$$\\nabla(Nf)(x)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\nabla\\Phi(x-y)f(y)\\,d\\lambda_n(y),$$\nand $x\\mapsto\\nabla(Nf)(x)$ is continuous on the open set $\\{x:|x|>2R\\}$;\n(b) [Decay bound] for every $x$ with $|x|>2R$,\n$$|\\nabla(Nf)(x)|\\le\\frac{2^{n-1}\\|f\\|_1}{\\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1}},\\qquad \\|f\\|_1:=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}|f|\\,d\\lambda_n;$$\n(c) [Scope] the hypothesis is compact support together with $L^1$-integrability; no boundedness of $f$ is assumed, and nothing is asserted at points with $|x|\\le2R$ (where the kernel singularity may meet the support of $f$).",
        "strategy": "Fix $x_0$ with $|x_0|>2R$ and choose $0<\\delta<|x_0|-2R$. On the full open ball $U=B_\\delta(x_0)$, every $y\\in\\overline B_R$ obeys $|x-y|\\ge |x_0|-\\delta-R=:c>0$. Thus both $|\\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\\le c^{2-n}|f(y)|/((n-2)\\omega_{n-1})$ and $|\\partial_i\\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\\le c^{1-n}|f(y)|/\\omega_{n-1}$ hold throughout $U$, outside the single null set on which $f$ may fail to vanish off $\\overline B_R$. Equivalently reset $f$ to zero on that set without changing any integral. The majorants are integrable; the kernel and its coordinate derivatives are continuous off zero and their products with measurable $f$ are measurable ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Restricting to each sufficiently short coordinate interval through any $x\\in U$, [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] yields $\\partial_iNf(x)=\\int\\partial_i\\Phi(x-y)f(y)dy$. For $k=1,2,3$ and $\\sigma\\in\\{+1,-1\\}$ use the relatively open patch $\\sigma x_k>r/(2\\sqrt3)$; these six patches cover because some $|x_k|\\ge r/\\sqrt3$.     "id": "post-sr-matter-models-and-evolution",
    "kind": "postulate",
    "title": "Adopted continuum matter models and their evolution equations",
    "domain": "physics",
    "statement": "Adopt, on top of the flat spacetime postulates [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] and [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], the SI conventions [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] and the particle premises [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]], the following classical continuum matter models on an open set $\\Omega\\subseteq A$: (i) Scalar field. A real smooth dimensionless field $\\varphi:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$, a smooth potential $V:\\mathbb R\\to\\mathbb R$ with values in inverse square metres and a constant $K>0$ in joule per metre have the field equation $\\Box\\varphi=V'(\\varphi)$ -- the Euler-Lagrange equation of the adopted local action density, with stationarity defined by the finite relative action for compactly supported field variations ([[lem-sr-scalar-field-euler-lagrange]]); the model's stress-energy tensor is the Hilbert tensor of [[lem-sr-scalar-field-hilbert-stress-energy]]. (ii) Dust. A $C^1$ rest energy density $\\rho>0$ (joule per cubic metre) and a $C^1$ future unit timelike field $n$ ($\\eta(n,n)=-1$) satisfy $\\partial_a(\\rho n^a)=0$ and $n^a\\partial_an^b=0$; the stress-energy tensor is $T=\\rho\\,n\\otimes n$. (iii) Perfect fluid. $C^1$ fields $\\varepsilon$ (energy density) and $P$ (pressure), both in joule per cubic metre, and a $C^1$ future unit timelike field $n$ satisfy the energy-balance and Euler equations of [[lem-sr-perfect-fluid-conservation-equations]]; an equation of state or evolution equation determining $P$ is part of the model and is not supplied by this postulate; the stress-energy tensor is $T=(\\varepsilon+P)n\\otimes n+P\\eta$. (iv) Additivity. The total stress-energy tensor of a composite system is the sum of the stress-energy tensors of its constituents (tensor-field addition on $\\Omega$). (v) Adopted observer readings and units. For a tensor physically assigned to matter in this model, all inertial components $T^{ab}$ have units joule per cubic metre. In length coordinates $x^0=ct$, an ideal observer with future unit direction $n$ and four-velocity $U=cn$ reads the numerical contractions of [[lem-sr-observer-stress-energy-decomposition]] as energy density $\\varepsilon_n=T^{ab}n_an_b$, momentum density $\\pi_n^a=-c^{-1}h^a{}_bT^{bc}n_c$ and rest stress $S_n^{ab}=h^a{}_ch^b{}_dT^{cd}$. Here $h(v)=v+\\eta(n,v)n$. In an adapted inertial frame these are $T^{00}$, $T^{0i}/c$ and $T^{ij}$ respectively, and the energy-flux components are $cT^{i0}=c^2\\pi_n^i$.         "title": "Linear and affine Lorentz maps, and the Lorentz group",
        "statement": "Let (V,eta) be a 4-dimensional Lorentz vector space (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia) with a chosen time orientation C^+ (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets), and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model). (a) A linear Lorentz map is a linear map L: V -> V such that eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V. The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted O(V,eta). (b) If (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is an ordered eta-orthonormal basis of V (lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis), eta_0 := diag(-1,1,1,1) is the matrix of eta in it, and M is the matrix of L in that basis (def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map), then L is a linear Lorentz map if and only if M^T eta_0 M = eta_0; every linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, and the condition does not depend on the eta-orthonormal basis used. (c) A linear Lorentz map L is proper if det L = +1 and orthochronous if L(C^+) = C^+; the set of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps is denoted SO^+(V,eta). O(V,eta) is called the (full) Lorentz group of (V,eta) and SO^+(V,eta) the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; that these are groups under composition is proved in lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure. (d) An affine Lorentz map is a map F: A -> A for which there exist p_0 in A and a linear Lorentz map L with F(p_0 + v) = F(p_0) + L v for all v in V; equivalently F(p) = F(p_0) + L(p - p_0) for all p in A, and L is then unique. F is called proper (resp. orthochronous) when L is. If x is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x(F(p)) = M x(p) + b for all p, where M is the matrix of L in the frame's ordered basis and b := x(F(o)) - M x(o) in R^4.         "statement": "Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), and let x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) be its coordinates, so that a vector is written x = x^0 e_0 + x^1 e_1 + x^2 e_2 + x^3 e_3 and the spatial part is the coordinate column x_vec = (x^1,x^2,x^3) of R^3 with its standard Euclidean structure (def-euclidean-inner-product).         "statement": "Let (V,eta) be the Lorentz vector space and let (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an ordered eta-orthonormal basis with eta_0 = diag(-1,1,1,1). For a linear map K: V -> V with matrix M in this basis, the following are equivalent: (a) eta(Kv,w) + eta(v,Kw) = 0 for all v,w in V; (b) M^T eta_0 + eta_0 M = 0; (c) writing M in the block form M = [[0, u^T],[u, Omega]] with u in R^3 and Omega a 3x3 real matrix, one has Omega^T = -Omega. The set g := {K : eta(Kv,w) + eta(v,Kw) = 0 for all v,w} is a 6-dimensional linear subspace of the space of linear maps V -> V.         "statement": "Assume the memory branch of the material-closure postulate [[post-em-material-closure]] in a material rest frame, and assume the hypotheses of the mathematical suppliers [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] and [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]]: Countable Choice for the smooth comparison route and, in the integrable branches, Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $E:\\mathbb R\\to\\mathbb R^3$ be the electric-field history in the material rest frame, read componentwise in its spatial basis ([[def-em-fields]]), and let $P$ be the polarisation response declared by the model.\n(a) [Causal response] If the kernel of [[post-em-material-closure]](c) satisfies $K\\in L^1(0,\\infty;\\mathbb R^{3\\times3})$, then for every bounded continuous history $E$ the response $P(t)=\\varepsilon_0\\int_0^\\infty K(s)E(t-s)\\,ds$ is well defined for every $t$, bounded and continuous, linear in $E$, and causal: histories equal on $(-\\infty,t_0]$ produce responses equal on $(-\\infty,t_0]$.\n(b) [Transfer function and dispersion relations] If $K$ is smooth with compact support in $(0,\\infty)$, the transfer function $\\chi(z)=\\int_0^\\infty K(s)e^{izs}\\,ds$ is entire, satisfies $\\chi(-\\omega)=\\overline{\\chi(\\omega)}$ for real $\\omega$, obeys $|\\chi_{jk}(z)|\\le\\|K_{jk}''\\|_{L^1}|z|^{-2}$ for $z\\ne0$ with $\\operatorname{Im}z\\ge0$ (with the whole-plane bound carrying the exponential factor $e^{b\\max(0,-\\operatorname{Im}z)}$ when $\\operatorname{supp}K\\subseteq(0,b)$), and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](b). If $K$ is locally absolutely continuous on $[0,\\infty)$ with $K,K'\\in L^1$ and $sK\\in L^1$, then $\\chi$ is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, obeys the stated growth bound, and satisfies the same pair of relations; an instantaneous real part $\\chi_\\infty$ may be added to the model, and the relations apply to $\\chi_{\\mathrm{total}}-\\chi_\\infty$ for $\\chi_{\\mathrm{total}}=\\chi_\\infty+\\chi$.\n(c) [Finitely-subtracted and polynomial branches] For each specified integer $n\\ge1$ for which the full hypotheses of [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]] hold for the declared response transfer function, its $n$-subtracted relations apply entrywise. These hypotheses include upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closed upper half-plane, the stated boundary $C^1$ regularity, holomorphy near the real subtraction point $\\omega_0$, and the order-specific growth bound $|\\chi_{jk}(z)|\\le C_{jk}(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set. A growth bound for one order $n_0$ permits every order $n\\ge n_0$ under the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses; it does not justify lower orders for which the required growth fails. Write $\\chi_{\\mathrm{tot}}(\\omega)$ for the full transfer matrix used in the response: it is $\\chi(\\omega)$ without an instantaneous term and $\\chi_\\infty+\\chi(\\omega)$ when the arbitrary real instantaneous matrix $\\chi_\\infty\\in\\mathbb R^{3\\times3}$ is present. The period-averaged work per unit volume is\n$$\\langle E\\cdot\\partial_tP\\rangle=\\frac{\\varepsilon_0\\omega}{2}\\operatorname{Im}(e^*\\chi_{\\mathrm{tot}}(\\omega)e).$$\nIt is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if the full Hermitian dissipative part\n$$M_{\\mathrm{tot}}(\\omega)=\\frac{\\chi_{\\mathrm{tot}}(\\omega)-\\chi_{\\mathrm{tot}}(\\omega)^*}{2i}$$\nis positive semidefinite. For any real $C^1$ history its exact instantaneous work split is\n$$E\\cdot\\partial_t(\\varepsilon_0\\chi_\\infty E)=\\frac{d}{dt}\\left(\\frac{\\varepsilon_0}{2}E\\cdot S E\\right)+\\varepsilon_0 E\\cdot A\\partial_tE.$$\nThe symmetric part therefore supplies the quadratic storage term; no positivity of that term is asserted unless $S$ is additionally positive semidefinite.         "statement": "Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\\varepsilon,\\mu\\in\\mathbb R^{3\\times3}$ (isotropic scalar case included) with $D=\\varepsilon E$ and $B=\\mu H$, and the conduction relation $J_f=\\sigma E+J_{\\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite and a declared external free current $J_{\\mathrm{ext}}$.
